name: Stellar
executive_summary: Stellar has run for eleven years as a payments network and, since 2024, has carried a modern Rust/WASM smart contract layer alongside it. The published TradFi score would improve if a dedicated spot trading vehicle existed; that single missing piece is what holds it to 65 against fundamentals that earn 68.58. The institutions that would use such a vehicle are already building here, with Franklin Templeton running a validator and using Stellar as primary tokenization infrastructure and DTCC targeting H1 2027 for DTC-custodied assets. On the agent axis the score is uncapped and lands at 65 on its own merits, with near-zero fees, no public mempool and protocol-native delegation on one side, and five-second settlement, no confidentiality in production and an agent toolset with no visible users on the other.

binding_cap.short_note: Capped by Regulatory Clarity Partial -- named in the March 2026 SEC-CFTC digital commodities release, with CME futures and a CFTC-regulated perpetual live, but no dedicated US spot vehicle; the Grayscale trust is still OTC-only.

key_findings: Stellar's regulatory standing is the one baseline check that lowers its published score. Based purely on its category-by-category performance, Stellar would score about 69, but with no dedicated US spot trading vehicle for XLM (Grayscale's trust is still traded only over the counter), its regulatory check is a partial pass and the score is held to 65. Its security check is now a fail: the most recent published independent audit of the core software covers version 25, while mainnet runs version 30, and the October 2025 data-corruption defect is still inside its two-year window. That check allows up to 70, so it does not lower today's score, but if a spot vehicle arrived the score would rise to about 69 rather than 70. Quantum readiness remains a partial pass: Protocol 30 (November 23, 2026) added post-quantum signature checks for smart-contract accounts only, while ordinary accounts still use today's signatures.

Regulatory & Risk is a strength at 84. Stellar has never been sued or investigated by regulators, has received two favorable early guidance letters from the SEC confirming it wouldn't take enforcement action on specific matters, and is stewarded by a US non-profit that publishes its own financial records publicly.

Real-World Utility scores 83. Tokenized real-world assets on Stellar grew to about $4.1 billion by the end of September 2026 and passed $5 billion in early November, by the Stellar Development Foundation's count, and stablecoin transfer volume reached $25.1 billion in the third quarter. The score is held back by concentration: a single issuer, Spiko, accounts for roughly half of tokenized value, and distribution still looks accredited and professional rather than broad retail.

Tokenomics & Supply scores 66. On the positive side: a hard supply cap, zero inflation since 2019, and transparent, categorized accounting of where the supply sits. Weighing against it: the foundation controls a treasury of roughly 15.17 billion XLM with no published schedule for when or how it might be released, and holders capture almost no direct value from network activity -- transaction fees are permanently removed from circulation rather than paid out to validators or token holders.

Decentralization is held down by three compounding factors, not just one. Admission to Stellar's most trusted validator tier requires unanimous approval from existing members of that tier, a curated process rather than open entry. Every validator on the network also runs the same underlying software (stellar-core), with no independently built alternative in production. And a small group of validators can vote to freeze funds, and has done so twice: containing the network's own corrupted data in October 2025, and freezing roughly 48 million XLM belonging to an attacker in February 2026. Both actions were publicly disclosed and aimed at stopping harm, which is the good version of this capability -- but it is still a capability, now written into the protocol itself.

Privacy & Confidentiality scores 38. Stellar has built basic zero-knowledge cryptography tools directly into its smart contract platform. OpenZeppelin released audited Confidential Token contracts in October 2026 described as ready for mainnet, but no mainnet deployment or usage has been confirmed, so they earn no credit here yet.

Operational Reliability passes on a record with no mainnet halt in over seven years. Contemporaneous reporting of a ten-hour outage in April 2021 describes an event that did not happen to the network -- SDF's own validators and public API went down while the rest of the network kept closing ledgers.

Settlement speed is the clearest structural concern for agent use. A Stellar transaction becomes irreversible once the ledger closes, which now takes a steady five seconds after Protocol 28 (September 2026) removed most of the earlier variation of up to about seven seconds. That finality is genuine, with no waiting on confirmations and no risk of reversal, but five seconds is slow for software that needs to act, check the result and act again. Protocol 30 added millisecond timestamps as groundwork for faster ledgers; the five-second target has not changed.

Economic Predictability is Stellar's strongest category at 78. There's no public staging area where pending transactions can be seen and front-run, tied fees are broken randomly rather than by who pays more, and during a fee surge everyone pays the same clearing price rather than bidding against each other. Validators also earn no fees, no staking rewards, and can't profit by reordering transactions. The score is held down by the same freezing capability noted above: a validator group can freeze accounts, and has.

Composability & Atomicity (72) is a split result. Stellar's original payment layer is excellent at this: up to 100 steps can be bundled into a single transaction that either fully succeeds or fully fails, with nothing left half-done and no helper contract needed. The newer smart contract layer does not join up with it the same way -- a contract call cannot be bundled with those payment steps in one transaction. Developers work around it by routing everything through a contract, which works and is the standard pattern here, but it is extra work that some networks do not ask for.

Agent Tooling (63) is capability without evidence of demand. Stellar has built a genuinely complete set of tools for AI agents: a server that lets an agent query the network directly, an official library of agent instructions covering most of the stack, and two separate standards for machine-to-machine payments. Building that before the demand arrives is a defensible bet. What is missing is anyone visibly using it -- no published usage figures, no named projects running in production, and no record of agent payments actually settling here. Scored as readiness rather than adoption, and it will move up quickly if real traffic appears.

Agent Identity & Compliance scores 58, splitting into a real strength and a real gap. The strength: Stellar has genuine tools for controlling what an agent can do, including signers that can enforce spending limits, address allow-lists, and time windows, plus newer protocol features (CAP-71 and CAP-72) purpose-built for this kind of delegation. The gap: there's no registry for identifying which agent is which, no standard way to formally link an agent back to the human or organization that controls it, and no system for issuing verifiable credentials to agents.

Security Posture scores 58. The most recent published independent audit of Stellar's core software covers version 25, while mainnet now runs version 30 after five upgrades, including a new account-freeze mechanism and post-quantum signature checks built on a library with no published independent review. Versions 28 and 29 fixed fourteen vulnerabilities, none exploited, with published security notes.

watch_items: A live, dedicated US spot trading vehicle for XLM is the single highest-impact pending event for this chain. It would lift the regulatory check, and the published score would rise to about 69, limited by the security check's ceiling of 70. Grayscale's Stellar trust (GXLM, about $27 million) has a registration statement on file to list on NYSE Arca; it has not become effective.

Security audits: the most recent published independent audit of stellar-core covers version 25 (February 2026), while mainnet runs version 30. A published audit covering the current code, including the CAP-77 freeze and CAP-87 post-quantum functions, would restore one of the two missing security criteria. The October 2025 data-corruption defect reaches two years in October 2027.

Post-quantum: Protocol 30 (November 23, 2026) lets smart-contract accounts verify ML-DSA signatures. Ordinary accounts, which hold most XLM, still use Ed25519; quantum-safe signers for them are planned for 2027 in the Stellar Development Foundation's roadmap. Wallets or custodians actually deploying ML-DSA-protected accounts would be the next step to watch.

Confidential Tokens: OpenZeppelin's audited contracts were released in October 2026 as ready for mainnet. A confirmed mainnet deployment with real usage would raise Privacy & Confidentiality on both frameworks.

Network activity: daily active addresses fell from about 115,000 in August 2026 to roughly 43,000-46,000 in November, and stablecoin supply also declined, while payment and tokenized-asset volume grew. Whether user breadth recovers bears on On-Chain Health.
DTCC's tokenization service lists Stellar for 2027, and Securitize and U.S. Bank's USBDC are announced or in pilot. Each earns credit only once it is live in production.

Every validator runs the same software (stellar-core), and the February 2026 data-provider outage showed the same pattern on the read side. A genuinely independent second implementation would be grounds to raise the relevant scores.
